To demonize someone or something means to portray them as evil, dangerous, or wicked — especially in a way that is unfair, exaggerated, or dishonest — in order to make others fear, hate, or distrust them.

Think of it this way: a demon is a creature of pure evil. When you demonize something, you are essentially painting it with that same brush — making it look like a monster in people's eyes, even if it isn't really one.

There are two things happening at once when someone demonizes a target:

  1. A false or twisted picture is being created. The portrayal is either completely untrue, heavily exaggerated, or strips away all the good or neutral qualities of the target, leaving only the worst possible image.
  2. That picture is being spread to an audience. Demonizing is not just a private thought. It's an act of influence. The person doing it wants others to see the target as evil or dangerous.

So, demonizing is less about what something is and more about how it is made to look to the public.

Almost anything can be demonized — the word is very flexible:

  • A person: A politician might demonize their opponent by constantly calling them a threat to the country, even without real evidence.
  • A group of people: History is full of examples where governments or media demonized ethnic, religious, or social groups — portraying them as criminals or enemies — to turn the public against them.
  • A country: During wars or political conflicts, nations often demonize each other, showing the other side as savage or evil in newspapers and broadcasts.
  • An idea or belief: A movement can be demonized by critics who focus only on its most extreme examples and ignore everything else.
  • A food, substance, or product: In health debates, things like sugar, fat, or certain medicines are sometimes demonized — treated as purely harmful when the reality is more complex.

This is the most important thing to understand. Demonizing is not the same as honest criticism.

  • If a politician is corrupt and you say they are corrupt with proof, that is criticism — it is fair and based on facts.
  • But if you take that same politician and repeatedly call them a monster, a devil, a destroyer of everything good, and you ignore any of their decent qualities or the full context of their actions, that is demonizing — it goes far beyond what the facts support.

Demonizing always involves distortion. It takes something real (perhaps a flaw, a difference, or a mistake) and blows it up to monstrous proportions, while hiding anything that complicates that picture.

People and institutions demonize for strategic reasons:

  • To build fear or hatred in an audience toward a target.
  • To gain power or support by making others rally against a common "evil."
  • To silence or discredit someone by destroying their reputation.
  • To justify harsh actions — it is easier to treat someone badly if you have first convinced people they are a monster.

Propaganda, political campaigns, and sensational media coverage are common places where demonizing happens.

These will show you how the word is used naturally:

  • "The documentary demonized fast food companies without presenting a single balanced perspective."
  • "Leaders who demonize immigrants to win votes are exploiting people's fears."
  • "She felt the press had demonized her unfairly, turning a single mistake into proof that she was a terrible person."
  • "His speech demonized the opposition, calling them enemies of the people with no evidence."
  • "We shouldn't demonize screen time entirely — it depends on how and how much children use it."
How Strong a Word Is It?

Demonize is a strong word. It carries a clear implication of injustice. When you use it, you are not just saying someone said bad things about another — you are saying the portrayal was unfair, excessive, and designed to make people feel strongly negative. It implies deliberate or at least careless distortion.
Words That Are Close in Meaning

These aren't the same, but they live in the same neighborhood — knowing them sharpens your understanding of demonize by contrast:

  • Vilify — to say very harsh, negative things about someone. Very similar to demonize, but slightly more focused on verbal attacks rather than the image-building aspect.
  • Malign — to speak badly of someone, usually with lies or harmful intent.
  • Scapegoat (verb) — to unfairly blame someone for problems they didn't cause. Scapegoating is a type of demonizing.
  • Stigmatize — to mark someone or something as shameful or disgraceful in the eyes of society. More about social shame than pure evil.

Among all of these, demonize is the most extreme — it specifically evokes the image of making something look like a demon, which is the most dramatic level of negative portrayal.
To demonize is to unfairly and exaggeratedly portray a person, group, or thing as evil or dangerous, with the goal of turning others against them.
